analysis.one_liner: Ties federal housing loans for manufactured home parks to basic tenant protections for residents.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a House floor vote; it died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require owners of manufactured home communities to give residents basic protections—renewable one-year leases, 60-day notice of rent increases with a written justification, a grace period for late rent, and the right to sell their home in place—before they could get federally backed loans to build, rehab, or buy those communities. It also imposed penalties on owners who broke those rules and created a commission to propose stronger standards. It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of manufactured home communities, most of whom own their home but rent the land under it. The bill would have limited surprise lot-rent increases, made evictions and non-renewals harder without good cause, and given residents a fair window to buy the community if the owner decided to sell.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Manufactured home residents who rent their lots

how_it_helps.text: Owners would have to offer renewable one-year leases and could end a tenancy only for good cause listed in the lease, with written notice of the reasons [S3].

Any rent increase or newly required charge would require at least 60 days' written notice, with a written justification tied to the actual costs of running the community, and extra notice for larger increases [S3].
Residents would get a five-day grace period on rent, a 15-day right to cure a missed payment, and the right to sell their home in place rather than being forced to move it out of the community [S3].

If an owner planned to sell or close a community, residents would get 60 days' notice of the price and terms and the owner would have to negotiate in good faith with tenants who wanted to buy it [S3].

The protections would apply as a condition of federal financing: HUD could not insure a Section 207 park loan and Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac could not buy a community loan unless the borrower certified the protections for every community they own, and violations could cost an owner access to federal housing financing for at least two years [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Owners and investors of manufactured home communities, including investor-owned chains, who would face limits on rent increases, evictions, and lease terms as the price of cheap federally backed financing. Lenders in these loan programs would also face new compliance conditions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Manufactured home park owners and investors

drawbacks.text: The protections apply only to communities financed with these federal loan programs, so most existing parks not seeking federal financing would be unaffected—the bill raises the floor only where federal money flows [S2][S3].

Owners argue the notice, justification, and penalty requirements would make community operations riskier and could reduce lending for building or improving parks, which over time could limit new affordable lots—a cost an honest supporter would have to weigh.
Enforcement depends on federal regulators writing rules and on the certifications owners make, and the bill authorizes no new funding, leaving compliance policing to existing agency resources [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the residents affected, the protections address real and common harms—sudden lot-rent increases, eviction-related losses of home equity, and forced relocations. The cost falls on owners who would accept restrictions in exchange for federal loan access, and the bill's main limitation is coverage: it disciplines only federally financed communities, leaving the broader lot-rent problem in place. On its own terms it is a targeted, low-cost consumer protection.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Financial Services Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Brittany Pettersen introduced the bill on July 11, 2023, with Reps. Bonamici and Omar, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services [S1][S3][S5].
No further action appears in the record: no subcommittee action, no markup, no floor vote, and the bill expired with the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners and investors of manufactured home communities, who keep unrestricted access to federally backed financing and can continue raising lot rents and controlling lease terms without the proposed protections. Home seekers lose nothing directly, but they also gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Manufactured home community owners and investors

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all eight cosponsors were Democrats, and a Republican-controlled House committee took no action on the bill; there was no recorded opposition vote because the bill never reached one.

industries.industry: Manufactured home community owners and investors (including investor chains and REITs)
industries.note: The bill would have conditioned access to low-cost federally backed financing on tenant protections—renewable leases, notice of rent increases with justification, and limits on evictions. Owners would lose the ability to raise lot rents and manage tenancies freely in federally financed communities, which is precisely where residents' interests run the other way.

industries.industry: Lenders and originators in HUD and Fannie/Freddie manufactured housing loan programs
industries.note: The bill adds certification, documentation, and penalty exposure to these loan programs, which could shrink or complicate the market for community loans, while a pricing-incentive structure rewards lenders whose borrowers adopt stronger protections.

Stronger resident protections and a federal standard site lease could make home purchases in financed communities more secure and support the market for homes that residents own, though the bill's main effect on this industry is indirect.
